title: Unit 4 Review — Choosing the Right Tool

phase1.intro:
Two very different rooms in the workshop, and both boil down to the same skill: picking the right tool for a job you can actually describe.

Where do you want to start the recap?

topics.buttonText: What questions decide which storage tool I need?
dialogue: [[term:For storage]]: Do I need order? (List yes, Set/Map no guarantee unless Tree). Do I need to block duplicates? (Set or Map's keys). Position or label lookup? (List's get(index) vs Map's get(key)). Always sorted, or sort-on-demand? Only touch the ends? (Deque).

stickyNote.flavor: 🗄️ order, duplicates, lookup style, sorting need
stickyNote.definition: Choosing a collection: need order? need to block duplicates? position or label lookup? always sorted or on-demand? only touching the ends?

topics.buttonText: What questions decide which concurrency tool I need?
dialogue: [[term:For concurrency]]: Am I sharing mutable state between threads at all? If yes — race condition on a single value (synchronized usually enough) or genuine coordination (wait()/notify())? [[warn:Am I hand-rolling new Thread() for every task, or is this a job for an ExecutorService pool]] — almost always the pool.

stickyNote.flavor: ⚙️ shared state, race vs. coordination, pool or not
stickyNote.definition: Choosing concurrency tools: is state shared? is it a race condition (synchronized) or coordination (wait/notify)? should this use a thread pool instead of manual threads?

topics.buttonText: What's the throughline across the whole unit?
dialogue: [[fun:The throughline across all fifteen lessons]]: every tool in this unit is a trade-off someone already thought through — speed against order, flexibility against safety, simplicity against control. [[key:Knowing the trade-off is the actual skill]] — method names are just vocabulary for a decision you already know how to make.

stickyNote.flavor: ⚖️ every tool is a trade-off, already thought through
stickyNote.definition: Every collection and concurrency tool trades speed, order, flexibility, or safety against something else — knowing the trade-off is the real skill.

phase1.openingDialogue: Unit 4's whole skill is picking the right storage or concurrency tool for a job you can actually describe — not memorizing methods. ⚖️

phase2.explanation:
Conceptual review — no broken code!

Common misconception: "I should always use the most generic interface (List, Set, Map) everywhere."

Actually: Use the most specific interface that meets your needs. This makes your code more expressive and prevents unnecessary restrictions.

Example:
• If you need FIFO, use Queue (not List)
• If you need unique elements, use Set (not List)
• If you need sorted keys, use TreeMap (not HashMap)

Another misconception: "synchronized is too slow, I should avoid it."

Actually: Synchronization is necessary for shared mutable state. Avoid it by:
• Using immutable objects
• Using thread-safe collections
• Using atomic variables

Only synchronize when you need to!

phase3.openingDialogue: Final check! Can you choose the right tool? 🧰

mcq.question:
You're building a student management system. You need:
1. Fast lookup of students by ID
2. No duplicate student entries
3. Students should be sorted by name for printing

Which collection should you use?

A) ArrayList with manual sorting
B) HashSet
C) TreeSet
D) HashMap
E) TreeMap

Select the BEST combination.

phase5.trivia: The java.util.concurrent package — Executors, Future, and everything else this unit's second half touched — shipped in the same Java 5 release (2004) as generics, which is why this unit's two halves (Generics in 4.6, concurrency in 4.10–4.14) share a birthday in Java's own history, even though they don't feel related on the surface.
